name: Contrastive Embeddings
question: How do I make vectors fit my domain?
summary: Contrastive learning is how most embedding models are trained, and how you fine-tune one on your own data. The model sees an anchor, a positive (a true match) and negatives, and learns to pull positives closer while pushing negatives apart. Hard negatives, which look similar but are wrong, teach the most.
useCases: Specialised jargon: legal, medical, internal product names
Off-the-shelf models that rank near-misses above true matches
You have real signals: clicks, tickets, Q&A pairs

items.detail: question ↔ correct passage, query ↔ clicked result
other examples in the batch act as negatives

steps: Collect pairs from real signals: search clicks, support tickets, Q&A logs
Mine hard negatives with your current retriever
Fine-tune a strong base model with a contrastive loss
Compare recall@k with the base model on a held-out set
pitfalls: False negatives (actually relevant passages) confuse training
Overfitting to a small dataset hurts general queries
A fine-tuned model means re-embedding the whole corpus
remember: Pull matches in, push look-alikes out.
caption: The dashed ring is “close enough to retrieve”. Training moves the right points inside it.

steps.title: Collect anchor–positive pairs
steps.text: Take real signals: a search query and the article the user clicked, or a ticket and the answer that resolved it. “what is MTF” pairs with the MTF article.

steps.title: Mine hard negatives
steps.text: Search with the current model and pick a look-alike that is wrong, such as the mutual-fund article. Skip the very top hits: they are often true matches.

steps.title: Use in-batch negatives and a temperature
steps.text: With a batch of 32, each query also treats the other 31 positives as negatives. The loss is a softmax over similarities divided by the temperature τ = 0.05.

steps.title: Train: pull in, push out
steps.text: Each step raises the query’s similarity to its positive and lowers it for the hard negative, until the true match ranks first.

steps.title: Evaluate on held-out queries
steps.text: Compare recall@10 of the tuned and the base model on real queries the model never saw. Here it rises from 0.71 to 0.86.

steps.title: Re-embed the corpus
steps.text: A new model means a new vector space. Every stored chunk must be embedded again before the new model serves queries.

pros: Teaches the model your domain’s distinctions and jargon
Uses signals you already have: clicks, tickets, Q&A logs
Small open models tuned on your data can beat larger general ones
Hard negatives fix the exact confusions users complain about
cons: Needs thousands of good pairs and a held-out test set
False negatives in the data teach the wrong lesson
Can overfit and hurt general queries
Every new model version means re-embedding the corpus
avoidWhen: You have no real query–answer signals yet
The problem is exact codes or IDs (BM25 fixes that without training)

tools.name: sentence-transformers
tools.what: Contrastive losses, hard-negative mining and a trainer

playgroundGuide.scenario: A broker’s search confuses “MTF” (margin trading facility) with “MF” (mutual funds). You are fine-tuning the embedding model on one query: the right article is the positive and the mutual-fund article is the hard negative. Train step by step and watch the similarities, the softmax and the ranking.
controls: Include or exclude the hard negative from the training loss.
Choose the temperature τ and the batch size, which sets how many easy in-batch negatives each query sees.
Train one or five steps, or reset the model.

outputs.name: Similarity to positive / hard negative
outputs.meaning: Cosine similarity of the query to each article. The higher one is ranked first by search.

outputs.name: P(positive)
outputs.meaning: The softmax probability the loss assigns to the right article among all candidates.

outputs.name: Loss
outputs.meaning: −ln P(positive): InfoNCE, the quantity training reduces.

outputs.name: Training steps
outputs.meaning: How many gradient steps have been applied.

presets.name: Before training
presets.expect: 0.62 to the right article, 0.71 to the look-alike: search is wrong. P(positive) 14%, loss 1.953.

presets.name: Temperature 1.0
presets.expect: Same vectors, but τ = 1 flattens the softmax: P(positive) 5%, loss 3.022.

presets.name: τ 0.5, batch 128
presets.expect: 127 easy negatives take 95% of the probability: P(positive) 2%, loss 3.852.

missions.text: Train until search ranks the right article above the look-alike.
missions.hint: From the start, two training steps with the hard negative included are enough.

missions.text: With the hard negative in training, get the loss below 0.1 while search ranks correctly.
missions.hint: Keep τ at 0.05 and train about five steps.

missions.text: Make the training loss look nearly perfect while search still ranks the wrong article first.
missions.hint: Exclude the hard negative. Easy negatives are already far away, so the loss is tiny but nothing is learned.

practice.scenario: A broker's search confuses “MTF” (margin trading facility) with “MF” (mutual funds). Fine-tuning an embedding model on a few thousand real query-to-article pairs from search logs, each with a look-alike wrong article as a hard negative, teaches it that these are different things.

industries.use: Domain acronyms: MTF vs MF, F&O, SIP
Specialist terms that general models blur together
Learn from click logs which products truly match a query

practice.analogy: Learning to tell identical twins apart. Seeing them side by side and being told “not the same person” teaches more than meeting strangers.

library.name: sentence-transformers
library.what: Built-in contrastive losses (MultipleNegativesRankingLoss) and a short training loop for any base model.

samples.code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, InputExample, losses
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

model = SentenceTransformer("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5")

train = [
    # (anchor, positive, hard negative)
    InputExample(texts=["what is MTF",
                        "Margin Trading Facility: buy with partial payment",
                        "Mutual fund basics for beginners"]),
    # ... thousands more mined from search logs
]
loader = DataLoader(train, shuffle=True, batch_size=32)
loss = losses.MultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model)    # also uses in-batch negatives

model.fit(train_objectives=[(loader, loss)], epochs=1, warmup_steps=100)
model.save("bge-small-broking")

numericDrill.question: A training batch holds 32 (query, positive) pairs. With in-batch negatives, how many negatives does each query see?
numericDrill.answer: 31: every other positive in the batch acts as a negative, which is why larger batches often train better.

interview.question: What are hard negatives, and why do they matter?
interview.answer: Passages that look relevant but are wrong, such as a mutual-fund article for an MTF query. Easy negatives teach little; hard negatives force the model to learn your domain's fine distinctions.

interview.question: How do you know fine-tuning helped?
interview.answer: Hold out a labelled set of real queries and compare recall@k and MRR against the base model, and check that general queries didn't get worse.

mistakes.fix: Filter false negatives, for example with a cross-encoder
Use a held-out set of real queries

quiz.question: Your embeddings treat “MTF” and “MF” as nearly identical. What is the best long-term fix?
quiz.explanation: Training on real query–article pairs with look-alike wrong answers teaches the distinction.

quiz.question: A batch holds 64 (query, positive) pairs. With in-batch negatives, how many negatives does each query see?
quiz.explanation: Every other positive in the batch acts as a negative: 64 − 1 = 63.

quiz.question: Which are good sources of positive training pairs? Select all that apply.
options: Search query → clicked article the user stayed on
Support ticket → the knowledge-base article that resolved it
quiz.explanation: Real signals of relevance make good positives. Random pairs are not matches.

quiz.question: Mined “negatives” often turn out to be clauses that also answer the query. What does this do, and what is the fix?
options: It teaches the model to push true matches away; filter candidates or skip the top ranks
Nothing: more negatives are always better
It speeds up training; keep them
quiz.explanation: False negatives confuse training. Remove likely positives, for example with a cross-encoder.

quiz.question: Which make a sound evaluation of a fine-tuned embedding model? Select all that apply.
options: Held-out real queries never used in training
A comparison with the base model on the same set
A check that general queries did not get worse
quiz.explanation: Training pairs reward memorization. Held-out data and a baseline show real gains.

quiz.question: MultipleNegativesRankingLoss uses scale = 20. Which temperature does that correspond to?
quiz.explanation: Scale is 1 ÷ temperature: 1 ÷ 20 = 0.05.

quiz.question: A query has similarity 0.8 to its positive and 0.6 to one negative, with τ = 0.1. What probability does the softmax give the positive?
Which are warning signs of overfitting during fine-tuning? Select all that apply.
options: In-domain recall rises but general queries degrade
Training loss is near zero while held-out recall is flat
Held-out recall and general queries both improve
quiz.explanation: Memorizing a small set shows up as a gap between training and held-out results.

quiz.question: The fine-tuned model beats the base model. What must happen before it serves queries?
options: Re-embed every document with the new model
Nothing: swap the query model only
quiz.explanation: A new model means a new vector space; old document vectors are not comparable.

quiz.question: Why use a batch sampler that avoids duplicate texts within a batch?
options: A duplicate would act as a negative for its own match
It removes the need for positives
quiz.explanation: If the same text appears twice, in-batch negatives include a true match, creating a false negative.

quiz.question: Training uses only random easy negatives. The loss is near zero, but look-alike articles still outrank the right ones. Why?
options: Easy negatives are already far away, so there is almost nothing to learn
The learning rate is too high
The batch is too small to compute a loss
The model has too many dimensions
quiz.explanation: Without hard negatives, the loss never sees the confusions that matter.

quiz.question: Training with temperature 1.0 separates matches from non-matches only weakly. Why?
options: Dividing similarities by a large temperature flattens the softmax
A temperature of 1 disables the loss
quiz.explanation: Low temperatures such as 0.05 turn small similarity gaps into large probability gaps.

quiz.question: Which are good practices for mining hard negatives? Select all that apply.
options: Mine them with the current retriever
Filter candidates with a cross-encoder to remove true matches
Use the positive itself as a negative
quiz.explanation: Look-alikes come from your retriever; filtering removes false negatives.

quiz.question: Which of these is trained with a contrastive objective?
quiz.explanation: CLIP aligns image–caption pairs contrastively. The others involve no such training.

quiz.question: A team has 150 query–article pairs and wants to fine-tune. What is the best advice?
options: Collect thousands of real pairs first; 150 invites overfitting
Train for 50 epochs to make up for it
Skip evaluation because the data is small
quiz.explanation: Small datasets overfit easily. Gather more signal and keep a held-out set.

quiz.question: You only have (anchor, positive) pairs, with no labelled negatives. Which loss suits this?
options: A triplet loss that needs an explicit negative
Mean squared error on raw text
quiz.explanation: It treats the other positives in the batch as negatives.

quiz.question: On 200 held-out queries, the base model finds the answer in the top 10 for 142 and the tuned model for 172. What changed?
Which click signals are noisy and need filtering before training? Select all that apply.
options: Clicks on rank 1 driven by position
quiz.explanation: Short visits, position bias and bots are not relevance. Purchases are strong positives.

quiz.question: Re-embedding 12 million chunks runs at 2,000 chunks per second. How long does it take?
You want to fine-tune a BGE model with the recipes used to train it. Which tool fits?
quiz.explanation: FlagEmbedding is BAAI’s library for training and fine-tuning BGE models.
